question: Does hard binarization split Chinese glyphs into their radicals?

method.capture: GDI CopyFromScreen over the configured region, 2920x176 physical, 200ms apart during live playback
method.score: mean per-frame character similarity (Levenshtein over alphanumerics) against a hand-transcribed ground truth

paused.note: one static frame sampled repeatedly; all four variants read it identically and correctly (19/19 chars). Windows OCR is deterministic on identical pixels, and preprocessing is harmless on a clean, high-contrast frame.

live.note: 76% of text-bearing frames read differently depending on preprocessing, so the choice is not neutral during playback.

truthHandling: Ground truth was hand-transcribed to score the runs and is deliberately not recorded here; see this directory's README. Runs are identified by shape and background only.

accuracyByRun.background: blue, low contrast against white text

finding: Hypothesis 1 of issue #53 is not supported. Binarization is content-dependent, not uniformly harmful: it loses 4.9 points on run A and gains 15.0 on run C. Radical splitting appears under every variant including no preprocessing at all - a single ideograph was returned as its two components with the frame handed to Windows OCR exactly as captured - so the segmentation happens inside the recognizer rather than in our preprocessing.
decision: Shipped preprocessing default left unchanged; the evidence does not support a change in either direction. Issue #53 should proceed to step 2 (capture resolution) or step 3 (Microsoft.Windows.Vision.TextRecognizer).
sideObservation: Character accuracy on hard frames is 66-74%, so roughly one character in three is wrong before the text reaches the translator. That, not the duplicate filter, is the ceiling on subtitle quality.
manualStatus: measured; single episode, three subtitle runs, one machine
